title: Professor Helen X. H. Bao
notes:
Moodle version of Week 4, built on 2026-10-26 from the Week 1 Moodle deck as the format template, in the way Weeks 2, 3 and 7 were built. 21 slides against the 30 asked for. The earlier 79-slide deck is kept beside it (RE07 Week 4 - Infrastructure Financing and Deal Structuring.pptx) as the source of material; it is untouched and describes the earlier shape of the week, which was organised in blocks A to H around project finance, contracts, risk, capital structure, procurement and support.

SHAPE OF THE DECK

The first hour is broad and the second hour zooms in. Four survey parts, each at most three slides and each anchored in a paper or report that I read and whose pages I checked: project finance and corporate borrowing (3 slides, two of them on the Hyperion data-centre financing), default, recovery and risk allocation (3), procurement and the cost of competition (2) and guarantees and credit enhancement (1). The focus part (8 slides) takes one question, how a project loan is sized, priced and backed, through three models with an interactive page each: Leland (1994) on how much debt, the EDHEC Infrastructure Institute's work on debt service cover on how much margin, and Merton (1977) on what a promise to pay the lender is worth. The pages open on generic settings. Then the case (1 slide, headings only) and the summary. There is no thank-you slide.

NO CASE IS CONFIRMED FOR THIS WEEK

The week's guest, Steven Norris, has accepted the week but the topic is not agreed. The first hour is therefore broad, and the three focus models are general: each is something a real project, whichever it is, can test. The case slide lists the kinds of evidence that would let the class test each model, not a case.

DATA CENTRES

The week's aspect of the course thread on data centres is how a project is financed when the tenant is a strong credit and the asset is not: the Hyperion financing of Meta and Blue Owl, in slides 4 and 5. Week 3 slide 7 gave its capital stack, and these slides do not repeat that. They take the lease, the residual value guarantee and the price of keeping the debt off the tenant's balance sheet, and the focus models revisit it: its cover of 1.12 and 90 per cent debt (models 1 and 2) and the guarantee (model 3).

PAGE NUMBERS AND WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED

Every source is cited in the notes of its slide with page numbers, which are the printed page numbers of the version I read, and each note states the offset. Several are working papers: Pinto and Santos (2019) is the EFMA conference version of 18 April 2019; Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis is NBER Working Paper 9757 of June 2003 (I recall it was published in the Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization in 2009; I have not checked); Decarolis is the March 2013 version; Currier is a September 2026 draft; Van Nieuwerburgh is NBER Working Paper 35865 of October 2026. The World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub document is the financial performance chapter of the Infrastructure Monitor 2024, which carries no title page in the file I have; I have taken its year as 2025 from the publication record, which should be confirmed. Not retrieved: Leland (1994) and Merton (1977), whose formulas I derived and checked numerically from their stated assumptions (the pages say so); Irwin (2007), the standard book on government guarantees; and a recent open source on partial credit guarantees, so slide 11 uses a 2018 Inter-American Development Bank note and says so. The Hyperion figures are the paper's, and the paper cites the Standard and Poor's pre-sale report, which I have not seen.

title: Lecture Outline
notes:
The outline follows the order of the week: how a project chooses between its own financing and the sponsor's, what default and recovery look like and how risk is allocated, how procurement shapes price, how public support is given, and then the focus of the hour, three models of a project loan. The last item is the case.

WHAT WAS CUT OR COMPRESSED, AND WHERE IT LIVES

The earlier 79-slide deck (RE07 Week 4 - Infrastructure Financing and Deal Structuring.pptx) stays as the source for everything below. The mapping is by slide title, since I read the titles of that deck and not every slide. The definition of project finance, the comparison with corporate finance, the theory of separation, the validation, the history, the pattern of use and when not to use it (old slides 5 to 12) are compressed into new slide 3. The Hyperion financing (old slides 13 to 17) is rebuilt as new slides 4 and 5, and the block discussion (old 18) is cut. The special purpose vehicle, the contract web, the turnkey contract, availability and offtake, step-in, sponsors, advisers, the security package and conditions precedent (old slides 20 to 28) are cut except where new slides 6 to 8 touch them, and are the first thing to bring back if the case is about contracts. Risk by phase, the allocation principle, practitioners' views, hard-to-place risks, pricing of risk, environmental and social risk, political risk, insurance, force majeure and change in law (old 31 to 39) are compressed into new slides 7 and 8. The capital stack, debt sizing, senior facilities, bonds against loans, Islamic finance, hedging, equity timing, cost of capital and refinancing (old 42 to 50) are compressed into new slide 6 and the whole focus part, whose first two models start from old slides 43 and 49. Routes to award, auctions, tender failure, financial close, bidder economics, evaluation criteria and standardisation (old 53 to 59) are compressed into new slides 9 and 10. Funded and contingent support, credit enhancement, viability gap funding and blended structures (old 62 to 65) are compressed into new slide 11 and the third model. The two cases, the term sheet, the Italian water case, the financial model slide, the candidate cases and the alternative running order (old 68 to 77) are replaced by the case slide and the notes; the Italian water case, which old slide 72 says Week 6 picks up, should be checked against Week 6 before it is dropped for good.

title: Project Finance and Corporate Bonds
notes:
THE FIGURE

Pinto and Santos (2019), Table 3, printed page 36: deals closed by borrowers in 19 European countries between 2000 and 2016. The left panel is the weighted average maturity in years (project finance 14.57, asset securitisation 16.57, corporate bonds 8.80) and the right panel the weighted average spread in basis points over the benchmark (project finance 222.28, asset securitisation 63.57, corporate bonds 235.63). The spread is the deal's economic cost of credit at closing, weighted across tranches (page 16).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The sample has 583 project finance deals worth EUR 145 billion, 168 asset securitisation deals and 3,949 corporate bond deals (page 4). Project finance borrowers took money for much longer than corporate bond issuers, with more tranches (2.04 against 1.33) and slightly more banks (5.05 against 4.48), but at a spread that the authors find is not significantly different at the 1 per cent level from the spread on corporate bonds (page 16). The authors find that structured finance is chosen when information problems, agency problems and issuance costs make a plain corporate bond expensive, and that firms choosing project finance are less creditworthy than corporate bond issuers (abstract). Structured deals also cost more to set up and run: the average management fee is 45 basis points on project finance bonds against 22 on corporate bonds, and sponsors bear an average up-front fee of 69 basis points (page 29). This is the empirical background to the week: a sponsor does not choose project finance because it is cheaper per unit of debt. It chooses it for tenor, for the allocation of risk and, as slide 5 shows, sometimes for the effect on its own balance sheet.

CAUTIONS

This is the April 2019 conference version, which I recall was revised later; check the published version before quoting. The sample is European and covers borrowers that issue both kinds of debt; 49 per cent of project finance deals are to utilities (Table 3), so the comparison is not of like with like, and the authors' regression results control for firm characteristics, which the bars do not. The spread is a deal-level average across tranches and is not a like-for-like price of risk. Printed page equals PDF page.

SOURCE

Pinto, J. M. and Santos, M. C. (2019), The choice between corporate and structured financing: evidence from new corporate borrowings, working paper, Catholic University of Portugal, 18 April 2019, pages 4, 5, 16, 29 and 36 (Table 3).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The reason the sponsor chose project finance, in its own words, and the corporate alternative it passed over: the tenor, the spread and the fees of each, and whether any debt stayed on its own balance sheet.

title: Hyperion: The Lease as the Contract
notes:
THE FIGURE

A timeline drawn from Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), NBER Working Paper 35865, printed pages 8 to 10. The Hyperion project is a data centre campus of about 2.0 GW and about USD 30 billion. The joint venture, Beignet, raised USD 27 billion of debt in October 2025. Meta leases the campus through five four-year leases beginning in 2029 and running to the bond's maturity in 2049. At each renewal date Meta may terminate the lease for some or all of the campus; the affected assets are then offered for sale, and Meta must cover any shortfall between the proceeds and a contractually specified minimum value (page 9). The renewal marks in the figure are at 2033, 2037, 2041 and 2045, the ends of the first four leases; the paper does not draw the timeline, and I have placed the dates by arithmetic from five four-year terms starting in 2029.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

A project finance loan is normally repaid from a long contract with a creditworthy buyer, a concession or a power purchase agreement. Meta wants flexibility in a fast-changing technology, and lenders want long, predictable cash flows. The structure reconciles the two by chopping the contract into four-year pieces and replacing the long-term commitment with a guarantee of value: Meta can leave, but if it leaves it pays for the difference between what the assets fetch and a floor (page 9). The equity is a joint venture: Meta sold an 80 per cent stake to Blue Owl for about USD 2.5 billion and kept 20 per cent (pages 8 and 10). The debt is about 90 per cent of a USD 30 billion asset value, and cover of 1.12 (page 9). The lease and the guarantee are what the lenders rely on, which is why the paper calls it a template (page 11): a Meta and BlackRock joint venture, Sopaipilla, used nearly the same structure in July 2026 with USD 12.3 billion of A+ bonds (page 11, note 7). Under current US accounting rules Meta recognises neither the future lease obligations nor the guarantee on its balance sheet until each takes effect, although one of the two will materialise for certain (page 9). Moody's estimates that hyperscalers have about USD 970 billion of lease commitments, of which about USD 660 billion are future leases not yet on balance sheets (page 9).

CAUTIONS

The figures are the paper's and the paper cites the Standard and Poor's pre-sale report, which I have not seen. The Week 3 deck (slide 7) shows the capital stack and these figures; this slide adds the lease and the guarantee. The characterisation as the largest investment-grade corporate issuance in US history is the paper's. Printed page equals PDF page less two.

SOURCE

Van Nieuwerburgh, S. (2026), Financing the AI buildout, NBER Working Paper 35865, October 2026, pages 8 to 11 and Figure 2 (page 10).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

A project in which the revenue contract is shorter than the loan, or a buyer's guarantee stands in for a long contract, with the terms of the guarantee and what each party said it was for.
text: Hyperion: The Lease as the Contract 4 The vehicle: a joint venture, 80 per cent Blue Owl, 20 per cent Meta, with USD 27 billion of debt on about USD 30 billion of assets The revenue: five four-year leases from 2029 to the bond's maturity in 2049; Meta may end each The guarantee: if Meta leaves, it covers any shortfall between the sale and a minimum value The accounting: neither the lease nor the guarantee is on Meta's balance sheet until it takes effect Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), NBER Working Paper 35865, pages 8 to 11 and Figure 2. Timeline drawn from the five four-year leases starting in 2029; the renewal dates are my arithmetic.

title: Hyperion: Project Debt against Corporate Debt
notes:
THE TABLE

The comparison the paper draws on pages 9 to 11, laid out as a table. Meta could borrow on its own account. It chose instead to place the project in a separately financed vehicle, and the paper puts a price on that choice.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Corporate borrowing by Meta would have rested on Meta's balance sheet. At the end of 2025 Meta's own leverage was about 25 per cent using book equity and about 4 per cent using market equity, and its operating cash flow of USD 130 billion was at least 18 times its 2026 debt service (page 9, note 4). The Beignet debt, by contrast, rests on cash flow through the lease and the guarantee. It was rated A+ by Standard and Poor's, one notch below Meta's own corporate rating, at about 90 per cent of asset value and cover of 1.12 (pages 8 and 9). It was issued at a yield of 6.58 per cent, at least 100 basis points above what Meta would likely have paid on comparable unsecured debt, which the paper puts at more than USD 5 billion of additional interest over the life of the financing, borne ultimately by Meta through its lease payments (page 10). The paper's conclusion is that the economic rationale for Meta is not cheaper financing but preservation of an asset-light corporate profile: the structure avoids adding the full amount of assets and debt to Meta's balance sheet and limits the effect on its reported capital intensity, leverage and credit metrics (pages 10 and 11). That is the same result as Pinto and Santos on the previous slides: project finance is not chosen for price. The paper adds a market signal: between 21 November 2025 and 22 July 2026 five-year credit default swap spreads on all five hyperscalers widened (Meta from 56.1 to 80.2 basis points), which the paper reads as investors pricing the opacity of off-balance-sheet commitments (page 11, note 8).

CAUTIONS

The 100 basis point difference is the paper's estimate of what Meta would have paid; no unsecured Meta issue at the time is quoted. The two columns measure leverage differently (corporate leverage against equity, project leverage against asset value), so the numbers show the order of magnitude, not a like-for-like comparison. Printed page equals PDF page less two.

SOURCE

Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), NBER Working Paper 35865, pages 8 to 11 (including notes 4, 7 and 8).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

For a project on or off the sponsor's balance sheet: what the sponsor would have paid to borrow itself, what the project paid, and what it got for the difference.

title: Default and Recovery in Infrastructure Debt
notes:
THE FIGURE

World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, financial performance chapter. Left panel, page 22 (Moody's 2023a and 2023b): cumulative default by year 10 for rated infrastructure debt originated from 1995 to 2023, global 4.3 per cent and low- and middle-income countries 13.6 per cent, and for unrated project finance infrastructure loans originated from 1983 to 2021, global 4.3 per cent and low- and middle-income countries 5.9 per cent. Right panel, page 18: Moody's average ultimate recovery rate on unrated project finance loans originated from 1983 to 2021, 84 per cent for infrastructure in high-income and in low- and middle-income countries alike, against 66 per cent (high-income) and 71 per cent (low- and middle-income) for non-infrastructure project finance loans.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

A project loan is a long claim on a single asset, so its history of default and recovery is the evidence the lenders' pricing rests on. Infrastructure debt rated investment grade had cumulative default below 2 per cent even over ten years, and infrastructure debt rated below investment grade defaulted less than non-financial corporate debt of the same grade, by a factor of at least one and a half (page 16). About 80 per cent of rated infrastructure debt was investment grade, against about 40 per cent of rated non-financial corporate debt, though it is hard for a project to obtain a rating in the first place (page 17). When infrastructure debt did default, recovery was higher than for corporates: trading-price recovery of 70 per cent for senior secured infrastructure debt against 55 per cent for corporates (page 18). The default rate in low- and middle-income countries is about three times the global figure for rated debt and about 1.4 times for unrated project loans (page 22). These numbers are the reference point for the models: the cover model asks what base-case margin gives a default frequency of this order, and the guarantee model asks who bears the tail.

CAUTIONS

The file I have is the financial performance chapter without a title page. I have taken its year from the publication record (the Infrastructure Monitor 2024, published in 2025); check the authors and year. The rated and unrated samples differ in period and in sample (about 1,000 rated securities of which 100 in low- and middle-income countries; 8,340 unrated project finance loans of which 1,038 in those countries, page 22), and the two default series are not like for like. The source's own text says metrics from different sources cannot be compared directly (page 3). Page 22 states the unrated global figure as a cumulative rate and the chart runs to year 10; I have labelled both as by year 10, which is how the chart reads. Printed page equals PDF page.

SOURCE

World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, financial performance chapter (Moody's, S&P, EDHECInfra and GEMs data), pages 3, 16 to 18 and 22.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The history of the project's own loan: whether it was rated, how it performed against the benchmarks, and what the lenders recovered or expected to recover if it ran into trouble.
text: Default and Recovery in Infrastructure Debt 4 Rated debt: 4.3 per cent cumulative default by year 10 globally, 13.6 per cent in low- and middle-income countries Project loans: 4.3 per cent globally and 5.9 per cent in low- and middle-income countries Grade: investment-grade infrastructure debt defaulted below 2 per cent over ten years Recovery: 84 per cent ultimate recovery on infrastructure project loans against 66 per cent for others in high-income countries World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, financial performance chapter, pages 18 and 22 (Moody's data). LMICs are low- and middle-income countries.

title: Revenue Resilience and Default
notes:
THE FIGURE

World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, financial performance chapter, page 19 (Moody's 2023a): the five-year cumulative default rate of rated infrastructure debt originated from 1995 to 2023, by whether the revenue is resilient. Globally 0.7 per cent for revenue-resilient debt against 5.4 per cent for debt that is not (eight times as high); in low- and middle-income countries 5.6 per cent against 10.3 per cent.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Moody's defines revenue-resilient infrastructure as availability-based public-private partnerships and regulated corporate infrastructure, meaning regulated electric and gas companies and regulated water utilities (pages 3 and 19). Debt on assets with such revenue had far lower default than debt on unregulated utilities, transport corporates and project finance other than availability-based PPPs. Availability-based PPPs had the lowest default rate of all, a ten-year cumulative rate of 0.6 per cent globally for debt originated from 1983 to 2020 (page 20). Revenue resilience is a design choice: contractual or regulatory provisions can create it, and governments can strengthen it through payment guarantees (pages 3 and 19). The same section records the other side. Where an availability payment is the only revenue, a default means the government did not pay, probably because it judged the project not delivered to expectations, which is harder to challenge, and ultimate recovery was higher when availability-based payment mechanisms were not used (page 20). This is the data behind the models' common theme: lenders lend more, and at lower cost, where the cash flow is predictable, and the guarantee model prices the support that makes it so.

CAUTIONS

The source prints the sample as 923 rated infrastructure debt securities mapped to 521 revenue-resilient and 421 non-resilient (page 19); 521 and 421 sum to 942, not 923, and I have not resolved the discrepancy. The revenue-resilient category mixes regulated utilities and PPPs and is defined by Moody's, so the contrast with project finance generally is partly a contrast between sectors. In low- and middle-income countries the source says the availability mechanism did not necessarily lower default, which it attributes to the concentration of payment risk on one public payer (page 20). Printed page equals PDF page.

SOURCE

World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, financial performance chapter, pages 3, 19 and 20 (Moody's 2023a and 2023c).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

Where the project's revenue sits on the spectrum from fully resilient (regulated, availability-based) to fully exposed (demand or merchant), and what evidence the lenders had for that.

Rated infrastructure debt originated 1995 to 2023.

title: Risk Allocation Matrices
notes:
THE TABLE

Selected rows of Risk Matrix 1, a new toll road developed as a design, build, finance and operate project, in Allocating Risks in Public-Private Partnership Contracts, 2016 edition, prepared for the Global Infrastructure Hub by the law firm Norton Rose Fulbright. The report has twelve matrices, five for transport, four for energy and three for water and sanitation (contents page and page 2), each showing for every risk who bears it in a typical transaction, in developed and in emerging markets, with the rationale, mitigation and the government support that goes with it. I chose five rows from the toll road matrix where the text states the allocation in words.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Land and site risk is borne principally by the contracting authority, which is best placed to acquire the site and to give the private partner a clean one (page 16). Design risk is the private partner's, as principal responsibility for the adequacy of the design against the output specification, although the authority shares it if the specification is so prescriptive that the private partner cannot warrant the design (page 19). Construction risk is the private partner's unless the work depends on infrastructure the authority must complete (page 19). Demand risk is the one that moves. In developed markets earlier projects placed it on the private partner, but traffic forecasts fell short and there were a few insolvencies, and over recent years it has become more common for the authority to retain demand and toll revenue risk, because the private sector will not accept it without extensive traffic analysis and protection against material adverse changes (page 24). In emerging markets the default has been that the private partner keeps demand risk, with possible pushback in some African jurisdictions and a possible subsidy from the authority if demand falls below a certain amount, for example in a cap and collar arrangement (page 24). The report says the appropriate application of risk allocation principles is what determines whether a PPP is bankable, meaning financeable, and whether it will last to the end of the contract (page 2). The lender's models on the next slides take the allocation as given and ask what follows for the loan.

CAUTIONS

The matrices are a law firm's account of typical practice for the Global Infrastructure Hub, written in 2016, not an empirical sample; the report excludes government procurement risk, private sector financial and performance risk and third party delay (page 4). The text in the PDF extraction loses which column is marked, so each cell above is stated from the rationale text and not from the grid. Printed page equals PDF page less three.

SOURCE

Global Infrastructure Hub (2016), Allocating Risks in Public-Private Partnership Contracts, 2016 edition (Norton Rose Fulbright), pages 2, 4, 16, 19 and 24.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

The project's own risk register or risk allocation table, with the contract clause behind each allocation and the one the parties negotiated hardest.

title: Thin Competition in Highway Auctions
notes:
THE FIGURE

Currier (2026), Competition and the Cost of U.S. Infrastructure, September 2026 draft, printed page 4 and page 6. Left panel: the share of state highway auctions with one to three bidders rose from 47 per cent in 2010 to 63 per cent in 2024 (page 4). Right panel: of the real price growth between 2014 and 2023, the structural estimates put the growth in variable production costs at 8 per cent and the growth in firms' margins at 45 per cent (page 6).

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The paper assembles a new dataset of the near-universe of state highway auctions from 2002 to 2024, with 1.3 million project-level bids (pages 1 and 3). The median auction draws three bidders and one- or two-bidder auctions are about a third of projects (page 4). Inflation-adjusted winning bids have more than doubled over two decades (page 4). Using out-of-state bidders' locations as an instrument, an additional bidder lowers the winning bid by about 10 per cent on average (page 5). A structural model of bidding gives a mean markup of about 0.2, roughly USD 25 billion above production cost over ten years, and of the 28 per cent real price rise over 2014 to 2023, about a third reflects project observables (projects becoming more complex), costs explain little (8 per cent growth) and margins explain most (45 per cent growth) (page 6). A counterfactual of one more bidder per auction saves about USD 350,000 per project, close to the 10 per cent (page 6). The paper links thin competition to large fixed costs of entering procurement and, even larger, of entering new state markets, pointing at procurement bureaucracy and regulatory barriers (abstract, page 1). The lesson for financing is that the price of the asset a lender is asked to finance depends on how the contract was won.

CAUTIONS

This is a September 2026 working paper and says it is a work in progress; the results may change. The data are US state road contracts, which are mostly design-bid-build with competitive bidding (the paper notes that of 40 countries the World Bank surveyed, all primarily used design-bid-build for traditional infrastructure, page 3), not PPPs or project finance. The paper's page 2 says the per-mile price of US transit lines can be up to double that of peers, while its footnote 1 puts the average per-kilometre cost of US projects 33 to 680 per cent above the UK, Australia, Canada and Spain, which I have not reconciled and have left off the slide. The paper does not say in so many words that 8 and 45 per cent are growth rates of the two components; I read them so from its wording on page 6. Printed page equals PDF page.

SOURCE

Currier, L. (2026), Competition and the cost of U.S. infrastructure, Harvard University working paper, September 2026, pages 1 to 6.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

How many bidders the project drew, how the winner was chosen, and whether the price the lenders financed was the price the work finally cost.

State highway auctions, 2002 to 2024; the decomposition covers 2014 to 2023.

title: Auctions and Renegotiation
notes:
THE TABLE

Three studies on what the winning bid in an auction tells the buyer, set out as evidence, setting and finding.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Bajari, McMillan and Tadelis examine a comprehensive data set of private sector building contracts awarded in Northern California from 1995 to 2000. Between those years 44 per cent of private non-residential building projects were procured by negotiation and only 18 per cent by open competitive bidding (page 1 of the text, PDF page 3). The authors find that auctions perform poorly when projects are complex, contractual design is incomplete and there are few available bidders, and that auctions stifle communication between buyer and seller, which stops the buyer using the contractor's expertise in designing the project (abstract). Decarolis studies Italian public works, using the different timing with which first-price auctions were introduced, and finds that at least half of the cost savings from lower winning prices are lost to renegotiation after award, because bids are not binding commitments; screening the lowest bid for its responsiveness prevents performance worsening but cuts the initial savings by a third and delays the award (abstract). Makovšek and Bridge review the evidence for the National Bureau of Economic Research volume on infrastructure investment and find that it does not match contract and auction theory's predictions well, especially for larger and more complex projects: negotiation and bundling do not clearly reduce renegotiation, because public clients cannot specify their full needs in advance, and high-powered incentives for on-time, on-budget delivery carry a disproportionate cost premium even in the absence of renegotiation (page 278). For a lender the point is that a low winning bid is not the price at which the asset is built, and the financing is sized on the base case that may be renegotiated.

CAUTIONS

The Bajari paper is NBER Working Paper 9757 of June 2003 and covers private building contracts, not public infrastructure; the authors draw implications for the public sector but do not test them. Decarolis is the March 2013 version and covers Italian public works of a particular type; the published version may differ, and I have not checked it. Makovšek and Bridge is a review chapter, and its own wording is that the evidence on larger projects is limited. Printed page equals PDF page less two for Bajari, and PDF page plus 275 for Makovšek and Bridge (the chapter runs from page 277 to 327).

SOURCE

Bajari, P., McMillan, R. S. and Tadelis, S. (2003), Auctions versus negotiations in procurement: an empirical analysis, NBER Working Paper 9757, abstract and page 1; Decarolis, F. (2013), Awarding price, contract performance and bids screening: evidence from procurement auctions, working paper of 27 March 2013, abstract; Makovšek, D. and Bridge, A. (2021), Procurement choices and infrastructure costs, in Glaeser, E. L. and Poterba, J. M. (eds), Economic Analysis and Infrastructure Investment, University of Chicago Press, pages 277 to 327 (page 278 quoted).

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

How the contract was awarded (auction, negotiation or a mix), how far the final cost and the contract terms moved from the winning bid, and who bore the difference.

title: Guarantees and Credit Enhancement
notes:
THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

This is the only slide of the week on public and multilateral support, and it sets up the third model. A partial credit guarantee covers private lenders against default on a specific portion of a loan or bond, usually for a public investment project and whatever the cause of default (Pereira dos Santos and Kearney 2018, page 31). A partial risk guarantee, by contrast, covers specified events such as government non-payment, and multilateral banks typically offer only partial cover, because they see the shared risk as limiting moral hazard on the part of the investor (page 26). On private estimates cited in the note, guarantees were then only about 5 per cent of multilateral development bank operations but about 45 per cent of private resources mobilised (pages 4 and 8, citing Betru 2017). The effect of support is visible in the default data of slide 7: infrastructure debt with resilient revenue, to which payment guarantees can contribute, had a five-year default rate of 0.7 per cent against 5.4 per cent, and in low- and middle-income countries 5.6 against 10.3 (World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, page 19). The Hyperion structure of slides 4 and 5 is a private version of the same instrument: Meta guarantees a floor on the value of the assets, and the lenders' risk falls to the tenant's. The third model of the focus part asks what such a promise is worth, and for whom.

CAUTIONS

The note on multilateral instruments is from February 2018, and the guarantee shares are private estimates from 2017; they are the most recent open source I could retrieve, and no 2024 or 2025 figure was found. A search turned up a 2025 section of the Infrastructure Monitor on blended finance and guarantees, drawing on Convergence data, which I could not retrieve in full; it says over half of blended finance infrastructure deals mobilised less than one dollar of private capital per dollar of blended finance, which I have not verified and have not used. Printed page equals PDF page.

SOURCE

Pereira dos Santos, P. and Kearney, M. (2018), Multilateral development banks' risk mitigation instruments for infrastructure investment, Inter-American Development Bank Technical Note IDB-TN-1358, pages 4, 8, 26 and 31; World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, financial performance chapter, page 19.

A CASE COULD SUPPLY

Any guarantee, indemnity, minimum revenue or value support attached to the project, with its terms, its price (if any) and how it was recorded by the party that gave it.

title: Three Models for Financing a Project
notes:
THE SLIDE

The focus of the second half of the first hour. A project loan has a size, a margin and a backstop, and each of the three models answers one of these questions. The pages are generic: they open on illustrative settings, not on any project, because no case is confirmed for the week.

THE THREE MODELS

Leland (1994) asks how much debt a firm should carry when interest is tax deductible and default is costly. At the settings of the page (15 per cent volatility, 30 per cent of assets lost in default, 25 per cent tax) the best debt share is 61 per cent of firm value (slides 13 and 14).

The EDHEC Infrastructure Institute's work on debt service cover (2016) asks how much margin the lender should leave between expected cash flow and the instalment, given that cover moves about with some persistence. At a cover of 1.30 and 10 per cent volatility the chance of falling below 1.0 in 15 years is 4.8 per cent (slides 15 and 16).

Merton (1977) asks what a promise to pay the lender is worth. A full guarantee of a loan of 70 per 100 of project value, at 15 per cent volatility over ten years, is worth 1.07 per 100 of loan, and 2.95 at a loan of 90 (slides 17 and 18).

HOW THEY FIT

They are three tests of any financing. Is the amount of debt consistent with how risky the asset is and what failure costs? Is the margin between cash flow and debt service wide enough for the volatility of that cash flow, and how persistent is it? Who holds the tail, and was it priced? The first hour has already given the evidence they rest on: default and recovery (slides 6 and 7), the allocation of demand risk (slide 8), and the Hyperion structure, which has 90 per cent debt (model 1), cover of 1.12 (model 2) and a guarantee of value by the tenant (model 3).

WHY THESE THREE

I chose them because each has a source that I could read or whose key result I could derive and check, each has a closed form or a fast numerical solution that runs in a browser, and each is a different kind of claim: a trade-off between a gain and a cost, a statistical description of cash flow, and a price. Alternatives I considered were a debt capacity model with a sculpted repayment profile, which is how real project models work, and a model of refinancing risk, which is the subject of the old deck's slide 50; I left them for the case discussion.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

For each model the kind of evidence a guest could supply: the leverage and its reasoning (model 1), the base-case cover and the outturn of cover over several years, with lock-up or waiver events (model 2), and the terms and price of any guarantee, and whether it was ever called (model 3).
text: Three Models for Financing a Project 4 Leland (1994): how much debt: the tax shield against the cost of default EDHEC Infrastructure Institute (2016): how much margin: debt service cover as a persistent random process Merton (1977): what a promise to pay the lender is worth: a guarantee as an option How they fit: a loan has a size, a margin and a backstop, and each model tests one of them

title: Leland (1994): Tax Shields and Default Costs
notes:
THE FIGURE

Drawn from models_w4.py at the generic settings of the interactive page: asset value 100, risk-free rate 4 per cent, payout rate 6 per cent, volatility 15 per cent, tax rate 25 per cent, 30 per cent of assets lost in default. The green line is the value of the interest tax shield, the gold line the value of the default cost, and the brown line their difference, all per 100 of assets, as debt rises from nothing to the whole of firm value. The dashed line marks the best coupon.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Leland (1994) models a firm that borrows with a permanent coupon, deducts the interest from tax while it pays, and defaults when its asset value falls to a boundary that the equity holders choose. The tax shield is worth more the more debt there is. The default cost also rises with debt, because the boundary moves up towards today's value and the loss of assets in default comes sooner in present-value terms. The brown line is their difference, and it peaks at the best coupon, here 3.70 a year per 100 of assets, which supports debt of 67.9 and equity of 43.3: a debt share of 61 per cent of firm value. At that coupon the tax shield is worth 14.9 and the default cost 3.6, so firm value is 111.3, 11.3 per cent above the all-equity value of 100. Default occurs if the asset falls to 33.8, which has a present-value weight of 36 per cent. The credit spread on the debt is 144 basis points. The model gives the relation between debt, risk and the cost of failure in closed form, which makes it a useful first test of any chosen leverage.

CAUTIONS

I could not retrieve Leland (1994), whose full text is behind JSTOR; I read only the abstract. The closed forms in the page were derived from its stated assumptions (perpetual debt, tax shield while solvent, bankruptcy cost, endogenous default) and checked three ways: against a finite-difference solution of the equity equation (largest difference 0.03 of one per cent of asset value), against smooth pasting at the default boundary (slope 0.004), and against a grid search for the best coupon. I have not compared my numbers with those in his tables and do not quote them. The model has one asset, permanent debt, no senior and junior claims, and no covenants; real project debt amortises. The inputs are generic. Python and JavaScript agree to 1e-13 on 300 random settings (check_models_w4.py).

SOURCE

Leland, H. E. (1994), Corporate debt value, bond covenants, and optimal capital structure, Journal of Finance 49(4), 1213 to 1252 (abstract read; formulas derived). The derivation is in the sources table of the interactive page capital-structure.html.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The leverage the sponsor and lenders chose, and the reasoning: what volatility they assumed for the asset's value or cash flow, what they believed would be lost if the project failed, and whether interest was deductible at the project level. A project with a leverage far above or below the page's is a prompt to ask which of those inputs differs.
text: Leland (1994): Tax Shields and Default Costs 4 The gain: interest is deducted from tax; at the best coupon the shield is worth 14.9 per 100 of assets The cost: default loses 30 per cent of assets; at the best coupon its weight is 3.6 The choice: equity holders stop paying when the asset falls to 34, against a value of 100 The best: a coupon of 3.70 a year, debt of 61 per cent of firm value, and firm value 11.3 per cent higher Leland (1994), Journal of Finance 49(4), the model; closed forms derived and checked (models_w4.py). Illustrative inputs: volatility 15 per cent, payout 6, risk-free rate 4, tax 25, loss in default 30 per cent.

title: The Optimal Leverage of a Low-Risk Asset
notes:
THE FIGURE

Drawn from models_w4.py at the generic settings of the page. The best debt share of firm value is plotted against the volatility of the asset's value, for three assumptions about the share of assets lost in default: 10 per cent (green), 30 per cent (blue) and 50 per cent (gold). The interactive page lets the audience change every input and shows the same curves with a marker for the current setting.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Two inputs move the answer: how risky the asset is and what failure costs. With 30 per cent of assets lost in default, volatility of 8, 15 and 30 per cent gives a best debt share of 65, 61 and 55 per cent, with spreads of 91, 144 and 317 basis points. At 15 per cent volatility, a loss in default of 10 per cent in place of 30 raises the best share from 61 to 72 per cent, and 50 per cent lowers it to 53. The page therefore makes the case for the project finance structure in one chart: a special purpose vehicle with a single asset, step-in rights and contracted revenue is an attempt to lower both volatility and the cost of failure. The EDHEC Infrastructure Institute reports that projects with little market risk are financed with a flat base-case cover and senior leverage of around 90 per cent, and that more highly leveraged projects show lower realised cover volatility, as Esty (2003) argued (EDHEC 2016, pages 8 and 9). The model, at generic settings, gives lower leverage than 90 per cent, which is useful: it prompts the question of which input a real project changes. Hyperion's 90 per cent debt sits behind a lease and a guarantee that remove most of the volatility of the asset's value from the lenders' view, but the cover of 1.12 is thin enough that the risk has been moved to the tenant and the renewal, not removed.

CAUTIONS

The model's debt is permanent and its default cost is a fraction of assets lost; the project finance literature would argue that step-in rights reduce that fraction, but this is my reading, and I have not found a source that measures it. Leverage in the figure is the debt share of firm value, which includes the tax shield, not of asset value; the two differ by the shield less the default cost. The comparison with EDHEC's 90 per cent is of a stylised model with a reported practice. The page offers a preset with 10 per cent volatility and 10 per cent lost in default, which gives 73 per cent. Printed page of EDHEC equals PDF page.

SOURCE

Leland (1994), as on slide 13; EDHEC Infrastructure Institute-Singapore (2016), Cash Flow Dynamics of Private Infrastructure Project Debt, pages 8 and 9; Esty (2003), cited there and not read.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The volatility assumed and the loss expected on failure, compared with the leverage actually used: what the sponsor and lenders said made the project safe enough for that debt, and which contractual feature (contracted revenue, step-in, ring-fencing, a guarantee) they pointed to. If the debt share is much higher than the page gives, the answer is in the contracts.
text: The Optimal Leverage of a Low-Risk Asset 4 Risk: volatility of 8, 15 and 30 per cent gives best debt shares of 65, 61 and 55 per cent, and spreads of 91, 144 and 317 basis points The cost of failure: with 10 per cent of assets lost in default rather than 30, the share at 15 per cent volatility is 72 per cent, not 61 Project finance: a single-asset vehicle with contracted revenue and step-in rights tries to lower both The evidence: senior leverage of around 90 per cent for projects with little market risk, above the page's generic figure Author's model (models_w4.py), after Leland (1994); illustrative inputs. EDHEC Infrastructure Institute-Singapore (2016), pages 8 and 9, for the practice of around 90 per cent senior leverage.

title: Debt Service Cover and the Lender's Sizing Rule
notes:
THE FIGURE

Drawn from models_w4.py at the generic settings of the interactive page: base-case cover 1.30, volatility of the log of cover 10 per cent, persistence 60 per cent, 15 years of repayment. The brown line is the base case, the blue lines the fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles of cover in each year, computed from the variance of the log of cover, which builds up from zero to the stationary level (the formula is in the page). The dashed lines mark cover of 1.0, below which the project cannot pay out of its own cash, and 1.15, an example lock-up level. By year 15 the fifth percentile is 1.10 and the ninety-fifth 1.53.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

The debt service cover ratio is the cash flow available for debt service divided by the debt service due, and project lenders size a loan on it: expected cash flow over the base-case cover gives the instalment. The EDHEC Infrastructure Institute (2016) collected 15 years of realised cover for more than 200 projects in Europe and the United States and finds that cover can be fitted to a lognormal distribution up to the 90th quantile for contracted projects and the 85th for merchant projects, that it is serially correlated, and that contracted projects have lower mean and lower volatility (pages 6, 8, 9, 32 and 37). A cover below 1 is an unambiguous definition of a hard default, and covenants set technical thresholds at levels such as 1.15 (pages 6 and 15). My model keeps the two features that matter for the lender's problem: the log of cover moves around the base case as a persistent Gaussian shock, with an overall volatility and a year-to-year persistence, and the probability of ever crossing a threshold depends on both. The loan is level instalments sized so that expected cash flow covers the instalment 1.30 times: at 6 per cent over 15 years that is debt of 747 per 100 of expected annual cash flow.

CAUTIONS

The pooled log-standard deviations in the EDHEC data are 0.289 for contracted and 0.316 for merchant projects (Table 4, page 32), but they combine differences between projects with changes over time within each, so they overstate the volatility of one project around its own base case; the page starts at 10 per cent and offers 29 per cent as an upper bound. The persistence of 0.6 is my arithmetic from a Durbin-Watson statistic of 0.857 on the residuals of a regression of log cover (Table 9, page 37), using DW as roughly 2 times (1 minus the first-order correlation); it is not an estimate of the persistence of cover itself. The EDHEC model has three states (safe, risky, default) and Bayesian filtering, which the page does not. Printed page equals PDF page.

SOURCE

EDHEC Infrastructure Institute-Singapore (2016), Cash Flow Dynamics of Private Infrastructure Project Debt, March 2016, pages 6, 8, 9, 15, 29, 32 and 37; the model is mine.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The base-case cover at financial close and the realised cover in each year since, with the lock-up, waiver or restructuring events. Even three or four years of outturn would show whether the process on the page, with the volatility and persistence it assumes, is close to what the project did.
text: Debt Service Cover and the Lender's Sizing Rule 4 Cover: cash flow available for debt service over the instalment; below 1.0 the project cannot pay The evidence: more than 200 projects over 15 years: cover is close to lognormal, persistent, and less volatile where revenue is contracted The model: at cover 1.30, volatility 10 per cent and persistence 0.6, the fifth percentile falls to 1.10 by year 15 The loan: level instalments at that cover support debt of 747 per 100 of annual cash flow, at 6 per cent over 15 years EDHEC Infrastructure Institute-Singapore (2016), Cash Flow Dynamics of Private Infrastructure Project Debt, pages 6, 15, 32 and 37. Author's model (models_w4.py); illustrative inputs.

title: Sizing Debt against the Probability of Breach
notes:
THE FIGURE

Drawn from models_w4.py at the generic settings of the page, with 15 years of repayment and persistence of 60 per cent. The probability that cover falls below 1.0 at some point in the life of the loan is plotted against the base-case cover, for volatility of 5 per cent (green), 10 per cent (brown) and 20 per cent (gold). The dashed line marks a breach probability of 5 per cent, the tolerance the page sets by default.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

At cover of 1.30 and 10 per cent volatility the chance of ever falling below 1.0 over 15 years is 4.8 per cent. A lender who will tolerate 5 per cent needs a base-case cover of 1.14, 1.30 and 1.69 at volatilities of 5, 10 and 20 per cent, and those covers support debt of 852, 748 and 576 per 100 of expected annual cash flow, at 6 per cent. The lender therefore sizes the loan by the margin, and the margin by the volatility of the cash flow, which is why contracted projects can borrow more than merchant ones. Persistence cuts both ways: at persistence of 30, 60 and 90 per cent the breach probability at cover 1.30 is 6.0, 4.8 and 1.4 per cent, lower the more persistent the process because it has fewer independent draws over the life of the loan, although a dip, once it comes, lasts longer. The Hyperion cover of 1.12 over 20 years gives a breach probability of about 5 per cent only if volatility is about 4 per cent (the cover needed at 3 per cent volatility is 1.08), which is plausible for a lease payment from a strong tenant and implausible for a merchant cash flow. That is the same point as in model 1, from the other side: the 90 per cent debt is safe if the cash flow is a lease.

CAUTIONS

A breach of cover is not a default: lenders waive, restructure or take over the project, and the observed cumulative default of 4.3 per cent by year 10 (slide 6) is not the same quantity as the breach probability here, so the comparison is of orders of magnitude. The volatility of 3 to 5 per cent used for the Hyperion comparison is my assumption: the lease is fixed, so the volatility of the cash flow is small, but the risk of the tenant not renewing or the guarantee not being honoured is not in a volatility. The chain used to compute the probability has 61 cells whose edge is the barrier, and agrees with a simulation of one million paths to within 0.0006. Python and JavaScript agree to 1e-13.

SOURCE

EDHEC Infrastructure Institute-Singapore (2016), pages 6, 18 and 19 (hard default at cover 1; distance to default); World Bank Group and Global Infrastructure Hub, Infrastructure Monitor 2024, page 22 (4.3 per cent); Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), page 9 (cover of 1.12). The model is mine (models_w4.py).

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The base-case cover at close, the covenant levels, and the realised cover. The sensible test is to find the volatility at which the page reproduces the observed range of outturns, and to ask whether the lender's margin looks right for it. If the project has contracted revenue, ask what the thin margin is relying on, a creditworthy counterparty or something else.
text: Sizing Debt against the Probability of Breach 4 Breach: at cover 1.30 and 10 per cent volatility, a 4.8 per cent chance of falling below 1.0 in 15 years Margin: for a 5 per cent tolerance the lender needs 1.14, 1.30 and 1.69 at volatilities of 5, 10 and 20 per cent Debt: those covers support 852, 748 and 576 per 100 of annual cash flow Hyperion: cover of 1.12 over 20 years is consistent with a 5 per cent breach chance only if volatility is about 4 per cent Author's model (models_w4.py); illustrative inputs: 15 years, persistence 0.6. EDHEC Infrastructure Institute-Singapore (2016) for the cover ratio and its dynamics; Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), page 9, for cover of 1.12.

title: Merton (1977): A Guarantee Is a Put Option
notes:
THE FIGURE

Drawn from models_w4.py: a loan of 70 due in ten years against a project worth 100 today. The blue line is what the project repays the lender as a function of its value when the loan falls due, which is the whole loan if the project is worth at least 70 and the project's value if it is worth less. The brown line is what a full guarantee pays, which is the shortfall, and the gold dashed line is what a guarantee covering the first 30 per cent of the loan pays, capped at 21.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

A guarantor who promises to make good the shortfall between a loan and the value of the project pays nothing if the project is worth more than the loan and the difference if it is worth less. That is the payoff of a put option struck at the loan, and Merton (1977) saw that it can be priced like one. A partial guarantee covering a share c of the loan is a put at the loan minus a put at (1 minus c) times the loan, a put spread. Two prices follow. The market value uses the risk-free rate in place of expected growth, and is the cost of replicating the payoff. The probability-weighted cost, which is what a budget that records expected payments would see, uses the real-world expected growth and is lower, because investors expect to earn more than the risk-free rate, so the project is less likely to fall short in the real world than in the pricing world. The gap is the risk premium on the guarantor's exposure. The lender who holds the guaranteed loan holds a riskless claim, and the saving in its interest rate is the same quantity again. The page uses a single loan due in one payment against a project valued as a tradable asset, which is a stylisation.

CAUTIONS

I could not retrieve Merton (1977), which is in the Journal of Banking and Finance; the formula is the standard Black and Scholes put, checked against put and call parity and a simulation of 600,000 payoffs (largest difference 0.013 of one per cent of the loan), and I have not compared it with his paper. The comparison between market value and probability-weighted cost depends on the real-world growth rate chosen (8 per cent on the page), which is an assumption. Real guarantees have claims procedures, caps, fees, time limits and a counterparty whose own credit may be uncertain. The Hyperion residual value guarantee is a put with the tenant as writer and a contractual minimum value as the strike (Van Nieuwerburgh 2026, page 9); I have not priced it, because its strike, term and the tenant's exposure are not public.

SOURCE

Merton, R. C. (1977), An analytic derivation of the cost of deposit insurance and loan guarantees, Journal of Banking and Finance 1(1), 3 to 11 (not retrieved; formulas derived from the option pricing result); Van Nieuwerburgh (2026), NBER Working Paper 35865, page 9 (printed page equals PDF page less two).

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

Any guarantee, indemnity or minimum-revenue support in the project: its strike (the amount or the revenue level guaranteed), term, who gave it, whether a fee was charged, and how it was recorded in the guarantor's accounts. The question for the class is whether the fee, if any, was near the market value of the page, near the probability-weighted cost, or zero.
text: Merton (1977): A Guarantee Is a Put Option 4 The payoff: the guarantor pays the shortfall between the loan and the project's value, up to the share covered The price: a put option on the project struck at the loan; a partial guarantee is a put spread Two prices: the market value uses the risk-free rate; the budget's expected cost uses expected growth, and the gap is the risk premium The lender: the guaranteed loan is riskless, so its interest saving equals the guarantee's price Merton (1977), Journal of Banking and Finance 1(1), 3 to 11 (not retrieved; formulas derived and checked); author's model (models_w4.py). Illustrative: loan 70, project value 100, ten years.

title: The Value of a Loan Guarantee
notes:
THE FIGURE

Drawn from models_w4.py at the generic settings of the page: project worth 100, risk-free rate 4 per cent, ten years to maturity. The market value of a full guarantee, as a share of the loan, is plotted against the volatility of the project's value, for loans of 50 (green), 70 (blue) and 90 (gold) per 100 of value.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

At 15 per cent volatility a full guarantee of a loan of 50, 70 and 90 is worth 0.19, 1.07 and 2.95 per 100 of loan. At a loan of 70, raising volatility from 8 to 30 per cent lifts the value from 0.01 to 10.49. At a loan of 90 the probability-weighted cost (growth of 8 per cent) is 0.53 per 100 of loan against a market value of 2.95, about 6 times as much, and the chance of the guarantee being called is 4.7 per cent in the real world against 20.4 in the pricing world. The lender's spread without the guarantee is 45 basis points at a loan of 90 and 16 at 70. A partial guarantee covering the first 30 per cent of a loan of 90 is worth 2.49, 84 per cent of the full guarantee's value, because the first losses carry most of the probability. A guarantee given free is thus a transfer to the project of its market value, which grows steeply with gearing and risk, and a government that books only the expected payment understates it by the risk premium. Revenue guarantees, minimum value guarantees on leases and tenants' residual value guarantees are the same instrument.

CAUTIONS

The numbers are for a stylised loan, with growth of 8 per cent as the real-world assumption; at a different growth rate the probability-weighted cost changes and the market value does not. The standard literature on contingent liabilities (Irwin 2007) makes the point that governments under-record guarantees; I could not retrieve it and do not quote it. The model is not calibrated to any actual guarantee. Python and JavaScript agree to 1e-13.

SOURCE

Merton (1977), as on slide 17; author's model (models_w4.py). Partial credit guarantee as a cover of part of the debt: Pereira dos Santos and Kearney (2018), IDB Technical Note 1358, page 31.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

The size of the guaranteed amount against the project's value (the loan to value), the volatility of the project's value or revenue, and the fee. If a guarantee was given and the fee was zero or small, the page gives the transfer to the project; if it was called, ask what was paid and whether the budget had recorded it.
text: The Value of a Loan Guarantee 4 Debt: a loan of 50, 70 and 90 per 100 of value has a full guarantee worth 0.19, 1.07 and 2.95 per 100 of loan Risk: at a loan of 70, volatility of 8 and 30 per cent gives 0.01 and 10.49 The budget: at a loan of 90 the expected cost is 0.53, against a market value of 2.95 Partial cover: the first 30 per cent of a loan of 90 keeps 84 per cent of the full guarantee's value Author's model (models_w4.py), after Merton (1977); illustrative inputs: project value 100, ten years, risk-free rate 4 per cent, real-world growth 8 per cent.

title: Three Models Compared
notes:
THE TABLE

The synthesis slide of the focus part and, if time is short, the one to keep. Each model answers a different question about the same loan, and a lender, sponsor or public body needs all three answers before it commits.

Leland (1994) explains how much debt a project carries. It predicts that the best debt share falls as the asset becomes riskier and as failure becomes costlier, and rises with the tax shield. Its evidence is the reported practice of around 90 per cent senior leverage on projects with little market risk (EDHEC 2016, page 8) and the lower realised cover volatility of more highly leveraged projects (page 9); its limit is that it is a model of a single asset with permanent debt and takes tax and default cost as the only frictions.

The EDHEC Infrastructure Institute's work on cover (2016) explains how much margin the lender leaves. It predicts that the cover needed for a given breach probability rises with the volatility of cash flow, and that contracted projects need less. Its evidence is the realised cover of more than 200 projects, lognormal up to the 90th and 85th quantiles; its limit is that realised cover mixes projects and years, and a breach is not a default.

Merton (1977) explains what a promise to pay is worth. It predicts that the value of a guarantee rises with the loan to value and with volatility, and that the market value exceeds the expected cost. Its evidence here is the logic of the instrument and the default and recovery data of slides 6 and 7, which show where the tail is; its limit is that the loan is a single payment against a tradable asset.

HOW THE THREE FIT

They give three tests of a financing. Is the debt consistent with the risk of the asset and the cost of failure? Is the cover wide enough for the volatility and persistence of cash flow? Who holds the tail, and was it priced? A financing that passes one only should be questioned. Hyperion is a worked example: debt of about 90 per cent (test 1 passes only if the lease and the guarantee make the asset's risk very low), cover of 1.12 (test 2 passes only if the cash flow is a lease from a strong tenant), and a tenant's guarantee of the floor on value (test 3 asks what that guarantee is worth, and the paper estimates that the structure costs Meta more than USD 5 billion of extra interest over its life).

THE LINK TO THE CASE

Students should arrive at the case able to put each test to a real project. The case section lists the kinds of evidence each test needs. The second hour is where they are applied.

A CASE SHOULD TEST THIS

Take the three tests to the case and ask which can be run with the data on the table, which need one more number, and which cannot be run.

title: Case Study: Topic to Be Agreed (Steven Norris, Chairman, Soho Estates)
notes:
AN OUTLINE ONLY

By design this is one slide naming the ground the case covers and leaving the discussion to the guest, Steven Norris. It states no facts about the case, takes no position and makes no claim, so it cannot spoil what he says. No case is confirmed for Week 4: the topic is not agreed, and the title says so. The title and the five headings are neutral and could stand over any project that has a financing.

HIS TITLE

The speaker note and his appointment letter (25 September 2026) address him as Chairman, Soho Estates. That was Helen's choice and not his own statement: his reply of 22 September emphasised his chairmanship of the council of the National Infrastructure Planning Association, and his website and Wikipedia still list a chairmanship of London Resort Company Holdings that he left in April 2024. Confirm with him how he wishes to be introduced before the slide is shown, and change the title here if he prefers the other.

THE FIVE HEADINGS

The project and its sponsor; the contracts and the risks they allocate; the financing and who lends; the public support; and discussion with the guest. They map to the week: the project and sponsor to the first hour's slides 3 to 5, the contracts and risk allocation to slides 6 to 8, the financing to the three models, and the public support to slides 11 and 17 to 18.

KINDS OF CASE THAT FIT THE THREE MODELS, WITHOUT CHOOSING ONE

Model 1 (leverage) is tested by any project in which the capital structure is known and was argued over: a case in which the debt share, and the reasoning for it, can be set against the volatility of the asset and the cost of failure, including a project that was refinanced, restructured or recapitalised, which shows what the lenders assumed.

Model 2 (cover) is tested by any project financed on a base case with at least a few years of outturn: the cover at financial close, the covenant levels, the realised cover year by year, and any lock-up, waiver or restructuring event. A project whose revenue was contracted and one whose revenue was exposed to demand would sit at opposite ends of the page.

Model 3 (guarantee) is tested by any project that carried public or sponsor support: a minimum revenue or value guarantee, an indemnity, a payment guarantee or a direct subsidy, with its terms, its fee or absence of a fee, how the giver recorded it and whether it was called.

KINDS OF EVIDENCE A GUEST COULD SUPPLY, IN ORDER OF HOW MUCH THEY ADD

A one-page summary of the financing: the sources and uses, the debt and equity, the tenor, the margin and the base-case cover. The risk allocation table or its equivalent, with the clause behind the allocation that was negotiated hardest. Three or more years of realised cover, or of revenue against the base case. The terms of any guarantee or support and what was charged for it. How the contract was awarded, how many bidders there were and how far the final cost moved from the winning bid. What is already public and what may be shown to students and later published, since Helen intends to develop each case for submission to Cities: Global Perspectives and a clearance is needed before drafting.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN

The case itself, the format of the session (guest lecture or case contribution), the date, and his title. This slide does not propose a topic; Helen's coordinating session will take that up with the case suggestions.

notes:
The same list as the Lecture Outline at the start of the deck, under a different title. There is no thank-you slide (Helen's rule, 2026-10-25): the summary is the last slide.

Run back through it one sentence per item. A sponsor chooses project finance for tenor, risk allocation and sometimes balance sheet, not for a lower spread, and Hyperion shows the price of keeping debt off the tenant's balance sheet at more than USD 5 billion of extra interest. Infrastructure debt defaults less and recovers more than corporate debt, most of all where revenue is resilient, and the matrices of risk allocation show demand risk moving from the private partner to the authority in developed markets. Thin competition raises the price of what lenders finance, and the lowest bid is not the price at which an asset is built. Guarantees and credit enhancement shift the tail to someone with a stronger balance sheet. The three models give three tests of a loan: how much debt is consistent with the risk and the cost of failure, how much margin the cash flow's volatility requires, and what a promise to pay is worth and who bore the cost. Then you meet a real project, and the question is which of the three tests it can pass.
